claims.text: Rapid solidification can produce a nanocrystalline microstructure in a magnetic high-entropy alloy.
Rapid solidification increases grain-boundary density relative to conventional slow cooling.
The relevant structural mediator is an increased density of nanoscale grain boundaries.
Grain boundaries act as pinning sites for magnetic domain walls.
Domain-wall pinning raises the external field required to move domain walls.
The increased field required for domain-wall motion increases coercivity.
A rapidly solidified nanocrystalline sample will have a higher coercive field than a matched coarse-grained, slowly cooled sample.
The predicted increase in coercive field is expected at room temperature when alloy composition and measurement conditions are matched.
Conventional slow cooling produces the coarse-grained polycrystalline baseline.
The coercivity-enhancing effect may diminish when grains approach the superparamagnetic size limit.
The effect may diminish when the alloy composition is not conducive to magnetic ordering.
The magnitude of the coercivity increase depends on alloy composition, microstructure, and processing details.
Failure of the nanocrystalline sample to exhibit a higher coercive field than the matched coarse-grained sample would falsify the hypothesis.
